title: Suicide in the Bible
lead: The Bible tells of a handful of people who took their own lives, among them Saul, Ahithophel and Judas, usually without comment. Later Jewish and Christian teaching built its judgments on these stories and on the command not to murder.

sections.b: The Bible reports several deaths by a person's own hand or request. Abimelech asks his armor-bearer to kill him so it will not be said a woman killed him (Judges 9:54). Samson pulls the temple down on himself and the Philistines (Judges 16:28–30), though many readers count his death as an act of war, not suicide. Saul falls on his sword at Gilboa, and his armor-bearer follows (1 Samuel 31:4–5). Ahithophel hangs himself when his advice is rejected (2 Samuel 17:23). Zimri burns the palace over himself (1 Kings 16:18). Judas hangs himself (Matthew 27:5). None of these accounts states a moral verdict on the act itself. Jewish law later forbade suicide on the basis of Genesis 9:5, with exceptions for cases like Saul's (Genesis Rabbah 34:13). Augustine argued that the command "You shall not murder" includes oneself, and his view shaped Christian teaching for centuries.

sections.h: Wishing to die, and God's response
sections.b: Several of the Bible's greatest figures asked to die. Moses, worn out by the people's complaints, said, "Kill me now" (Numbers 11:15), and God answered by giving him seventy elders to share the load. Elijah lay down under a broom tree and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). An angel woke him, fed him and let him sleep, twice, before God spoke to him at Horeb (1 Kings 19:5–18). Jonah asked to die (Jonah 4:3, 8), and God answered with patient questions. Job cursed the day he was born (Job 3) and was not condemned for his honesty. When the jailer at Philippi drew his sword to kill himself, Paul shouted, "Do yourself no harm! Every one of us is still here!" (Acts 16:27–28), and the night ended with the jailer's family fed and baptized. In each case despair is met with care, food, rest, company and a future.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians counsel today
sections.b: Older teaching was often harsh: suicides were denied full burial in both Jewish and Christian communities, and some Christians taught that suicide could not be forgiven. Modern teaching in both traditions is more careful and more merciful. Jewish law generally presumes that a person who died by suicide was not acting freely, under the pressure of illness or anguish (anus), so full burial and mourning are allowed. The Catholic Catechism (2282–2283) teaches that grave psychological suffering can lessen responsibility, that we should not despair of the eternal salvation of those who have taken their lives, and that the church prays for them. Many Protestant writers likewise reject the idea that suicide is the unforgivable sin. All these traditions still teach that life is God's gift and urge anyone in despair to seek help.
If you are thinking about ending your life, please reach out to someone now. In the US you can call or text 988. Elsewhere, local emergency services can connect you with help.
